items.title: Learning Generative Maps & the Rewards Guiding Them: Normalizing Flow Maps & Surrogate Reward Mixing
items.desc: Learning a generative model gives us a sampler for a data distribution. Adapting that sampler to a downstream task requires rewarding preferential outcomes typically in the form of scalar rewards or rankings that the model must internalize. In this talk, I will discuss learning generative maps as well as new methodology to exploit (multiple) rewards at inference used to guide them. I will first introduce Normalizing Flow Maps (NFM), a new generative modeling class which combine few-step generation with exact likelihood evaluation by learning invertible transport maps along a generative probability path. NFMs are centered around two matching principles: Pointwise and distributional matching…

items.title: Universality of Nodal Statistics of Random Matrices
items.desc:
Kyle Luh (University of Colorado Boulder)
https://simons.berkeley.edu/talks/kyle-luh-university-colorado-boulder-2026-11-02
Beyond Graph Laplacians

Nodal statistics turn an eigenvector into a geometric or combinatorial object by recording where its signs are compatible with the operator. We establish a central limit theorem for the nodal statistics of the k-th eigenvector of an orthogonally invariant ensemble of random matrices. This resolves a conjecture of Alon, Mikulincer and Urschel. To attack this problem, we develop some random matrix and combinatorial machinery that may be of independent interest. This is joint work with G. Berkolaiko.

items.title: Nodal Statistics for Graphs and Matrices
items.desc:
John Urschel (MIT)
https://simons.berkeley.edu/talks/john-urschel-mit-2026-11-02
Beyond Graph Laplacians

Given a symmetric matrix with a given sign pattern, what can the sign patterns of its eigenvectors look like? This simple question is closely related to the study of discrete nodal statistics and draws strong parallels with classical results in analysis for Laplacian eigenfunctions. In this talk, we will give an overview of the field, covering key results on nodal sets for graphs and their connection to known results and open problems in the continuous setting. In addition, we will discuss some recent progress towards a more complete understanding of the extremal properties of the nodal…

Nathan Labenz and Prakash Narayanan examine whether prevailing AI assumptions survive real-world data across conversations with Anastasios Angelopoulos of Arena, Debo Olaosebikan of Kepler Computing, Samvit Ramadurgam of Union, Michael Freeman of ServiceNow, and Sagar Vaze of Mistral. items.title: Release Recap: Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents
items.desc:
​Join Keenan Samway, Daniel D'souza, and Nouha Dziri as they explore a novel approach to multi-agent system design for scaling inference by framing team construction as a compute allocation problem. They demonstrate that strategic delegation—specifically assigning workers to planning rather than implementation or verification—can achieve near-optimal reward at a fraction of the cost, with a heterogeneous 17-agent team reaching within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost, thereby offering actionable guidelines for optimizing agent budgets under task, cost, and latency constraints.

It seemed like the news cycle had stabilized a bit when I started writing this, but then there was news about another major crypto security incident at Binance. items.title: Antoine Guedon - Surflo: Consistent 3D Surface Flow Model with Global State
items.desc: ​Geometry is invariant to viewpoint, which makes any collection of images a redundant encoding of a single 3D state. Existing feed-forward reconstruction models fail to exploit this: per-view methods emit overlapping, unaligned pointmaps that grow linearly with input count, while global-latent methods commit to a fixed, low-resolution output. We introduce Surflo, which compresses a variable number of unposed RGB views into K latent tokens-one global state-and decodes oriented 3D surface points by independently transporting them from noise onto the surface via flow matching. This frees the output from any fixed grid or token budget: the same latent yields from a few thousand to a million…

items.title: Luke Muehlhauser on the most important AI safety work nobody is doing
items.desc:
The US government spends 25 times more on military marching bands than on its AI safety institute. And that’s just one of the many institutions we’re missing as AI becomes more powerful and dangerous.
Aviation has the FAA to regulate safety and the NTSB to investigate crashes. Nuclear power has international inspectors and industry watchdogs. But for advanced AI, as Luke Muehlhauser puts it, “most of the institutions that need to exist don’t exist.”
Luke has worked on AI risk since 2011, and now leads AI governance and international policy grantmaking at Coefficient Giving. He thinks we urgently need organisations that can independently evaluate frontier models, investigate AI incidents, verify AI companies’ safety claims, and hold them accountable.
He also wants people to build more specialised organisations: one that tests whether AI systems are prone to lying or pursuing hidden…

items.title: Taking on ServiceNow: Coding Agents the Rest of Us with Serval Co-Founder and CEO Jake Stauch
items.desc: What happens when you put code-generation agents in the hands of enterprise IT teams? With Serval, you get a system where it's easy for everyone to be a builder. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with Serval co-founder and CEO Jake Stauch to analyze his company’s direct challenge to ServiceNow as the enterprise automation and service management system of record. Jake explains that by building an AI platform for enterprise IT departments with Serval, users can safely build while still safeguarding permissions by strict deterministic approvals and an audit trail. He also talks about ProServal, the company’s team that embeds automation engineers directly with customers in order to provide ongoing support and service. Jake also discusses how AI was the big unlock to taking on ServiceNow, why he’s betting on coding agents getting even better, why consumer is a window into what will happen next…

Joel Predd, Ben Boudreaux, and Matt Chessen of RAND's Center for the Geopolitics of AGI join Nathan to discuss their framework for maintaining freedom of action on the path to superintelligence. Analyzing seven strategic archetypes—including dominance, deterrence, co-development, and moratoriums—they argue that deep technological and geopolitical uncertainty makes defaulting to any single strategy dangerous. To avoid foreclosing critical options, their proposed approach calls for investing in long-lead capabilities like model verification, containment, agency evaluations, and an adaptable security architecture. At stake are decisive economic and military advantage, stable competition with rivals like China, and humanity's survival with agency.

items.desc:
Hill-climbing is easy, knowing what to hill-climb is hard. Making scores go up is expensive, but we have a much clearer playbook for it than we do for creating meaningful benchmarks at the true frontier of AI today.
Independent evaluation of language models is under-appreciated in how hard of a task it is. These groups are not just taking current models and certifying their scores, which is a technically involved task. This is their job if AI progress is slow. items.title: Why Silicon Valley can’t slow down AI on its own | Luisa Rodriguez
items.desc:
Two-thirds of Americans think AI is moving too fast. So do the people building it. So why the hell isn’t anyone slowing down?
We can’t tell when models are too dangerous. We mostly don’t know how they work. We don’t know how to make them do what we want. And our two main safety checks — testing behaviour and monitoring their ‘thoughts’ — are breaking down.
Yet we’re racing to build more powerful AI anyway, faster every year. And it’s only going to accelerate as AI itself gets better and better at building the next generation of models.
Earlier this year, OpenAI found its new model, Astra, was alarmingly good at hacking, and did something companies almost never do: paused its biggest training project. But it released Astra anyway, even though tests couldn’t prove if it was safe.
That’s the problem with leaving it up to the companies. We can’t trust them to act in our best interest…

Despite the field's maturity, recent models still struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution inputs and to produce sharp and detailed depth maps. In this talk, we revisit Marigold, a set of techniques for repurposing modern image generation and editing models, powered by the diffusion transformer (DiT) architecture, into state-of-the-art monocular depth estimators. Our recipes target single-step inference from pretrained multi-step flow-matching models, with quantization where needed, preserving…

items.title: AI Technology for AI Scientists
items.desc:
September 25, 2026 Tea Talk 
As the general capabilities of AI systems are developing, AI scientists are now confronted with one question: how should they themselves use AI for their work? In this talk, I'll present my current research aimed at providing some answers. Specifically, I'll describe progress on the use of AI for common tasks in scientific work, such as the reviewing of scientific papers, the forecasting of future events through judgemental reasoning, and the generation of scientific hypotheses from unstructured data.

items.title: Does My LLM Have Emotions Yet?
items.desc:
September 15, 2026
Claims that large language models experience depression, anxiety, or other emotional states continue to surface, alongside reports of "AI psychosis" in users who form intense attachments to chatbots. But what can we understand of these phenomena based on the science of emotion? This talk reviews what neuroscience, social psychology, and developmental psychology have established about how emotions function in biological creatures. I distinguish related but distinct constructs like emotional intelligence, empathy, and emotional contagion, and contrast deep and shallow affect towards untangling whether an emotion is felt or merely simulated. With this grounding, I discuss…

items.title: Andy Zeyi Liu - Semigroup-JEPA: Latent Dynamics Consistency for Zero-Shot Physics Generalization
items.desc: ​Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world models learn a compact latent representation of the world that supports prediction and planning, but their capability to learn physics and generate physically realistic dynamics remains hitherto untested. In this work, we introduce SemiGroup-JEPA (SG-JEPA), which extends the LeWorldModel framework by supplying the parameter governing the physics to the temporal model via action-conditioning and jointly training an encoder and predictor through an autoregressive latent rollout. To evaluate the model's ability to generalize out of distribution, we design dynamical tasks under different gravitational fields that, despite obeying the same…

This talk explores how AI-driven techniques can transform network data into actionable intelligence to improve efficiency, adaptability, and security. It highlights three interconnected research areas: intelligent congestion control, network traffic fingerprinting, and resilient computing systems. First, machine learning…

items.title: Your Ranking Model Is Optimizing the Wrong Thing with Zoe Weil - #780
items.desc:
In this episode, Zoe Weil, co-founder and CEO of Sequen, joins us to discuss how ranking systems can use live behavioral signals to optimize for purchases rather than clicks or search relevance alone. Zoe explains why approaches developed at data-rich social platforms don’t necessarily translate to retailers and how Sequen uses scroll speed, hover duration, and other in-session interactions to infer shopper intent without relying on user identity.

We explore the company’s large event models and its architecture of specialized models that transform streaming events into features for downstream rankers. Zoe describes the infrastructure required to serve dynamic rankings within milliseconds, why the team chose Rust for its backend, and how evaluation harnesses connect model improvements to business outcomes. We also discuss the tradeoffs between advertising and organic revenue, continuous…

items.title: The Changing Physics of Cybersecurity and Drug Development with OpenAI President Greg Brockman
items.desc: Technology has always been the fundamental driver of improvement for human quality of life. And with the recent rollout of advanced frontier models, like OpenAI’s GPT-6, humanity can now massively accelerate scientific discovery for its benefit. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil are joined by OpenAI President and co-founder Greg Brockman to discuss the company’s rapid progress across frontier models, cybersecurity, and scientific discovery. Greg shares how nearly 400 century-old math problems have been solved using its AI agents, and how the technology has the potential to transform other fields like biology in the realm of drug discovery. He also talks about how proactive, always-on AI agents like Dots impact modern productivity, why he believes the best UI is no UI at all, how cybersecurity is in a critical window of time to use peak intelligence to find and fix vulnerabilities in systems, and…

items.desc:
Title: Beyond Teleoperation: Zero-Shot Sim-To-Real At Scale
Speaker: Rose Hendrix, Maya Guru, and Rohun Tripathi (AI2)
Date: Friday, October 9, 2026

Abstract: Learning-based robotic manipulation currently depends heavily on high-fidelity real-world teleoperation data. Such data is effective within a fixed setting but scales poorly: it is costly to collect, and each substantial change in embodiment devalues existing datasets and necessitates re-collection. As robot hardware diversifies, this overhead increasingly constrains the field. I argue that simulation, properly designed, can serve as a durable and reusable foundation for robot learning rather than merely a stopgap for data scarcity,…

items.title: Learning long-ranged structure in English with Lindsay Smith
items.desc:
Lindsay Smith from Princeton University joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "Learning long-ranged structure in English: Code length and entropy dynamics during LLM training."

We use large language models (LLMs) to uncover long-ranged structure in English texts from a variety of sources. We test both open-weight models and a 1.7B-parameter LLM that we train ourselves, controlling the exact data the model sees during training. The conditional entropy and code length in many cases continue to decrease with context length at least to [Math Processing Error] characters, implying that there are direct dependencies or…

items.title: The Dynamics of Language Evolution from Humans to LLMs with Devon Jarvis
items.desc:
Devon Jarvis from University of the Witwatersrand and the MIND Institute joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "The Dynamics of Language Evolution from Humans to LLMs."

While many species have forms of communication, humans appear to have a unique capacity for language: we can express a seemingly infinite number of meanings by composing a finite set of words. The source of this ability remains debated. One theory, Iterated Learning, proposes that although the human brain has biases that favour structure, it does not have an explicit, innate capacity for language. Instead, language evolves over repeated cycles of…

items.title: From Connectome to Computation with Anthony Zador
items.desc:
Anthony Zador joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "From Connectome to Computation."

Animals are born with highly structured brain connectivity, which equips them with the ability to function well soon after birth with little or no experience. Because the wiring diagram is far too complex to be specified explicitly in the genome, it must be compressed through a ‘genomic bottleneck’. I will discuss theoretical and experimental results regarding the nature of the rules governing the genomic bottleneck.

items.title: How dendritic trees shape local learning and route credit with Houman Safaai
items.desc:
Houman Safaai from Harvard University joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "How dendritic trees shape local learning and route credit."

Biological neurons receive input through thousands of synapses on branching dendrites, yet artificial networks typically use point neurons trained by global backpropagation. Biological learning must instead rely on local signals. We ask how conductance and topology shape credit assignment, from local rules to anatomical routes. We first derive exact gradients for conductance-based dendritic networks with excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Each gradient factors into local eligibility…

items.title: Distinct mechanisms underlying in-context learning in transformers with Cole Gibson
items.desc:
Cole Gibson from Princeton University joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "Distinct mechanisms underlying in-context learning in transformers."

Modern distributed networks, notably transformers, acquire a remarkable ability (termed `in-context learning’) to adapt their computation to input statistics, such that a fixed network can be applied to data from a broad range of systems. Here, we provide a complete mechanistic characterization of this behavior in transformers trained on a finite set S of discrete Markov chains. The transformer displays four algorithmic phases, characterized by whether the network memorizes…

items.title: Emergent Traveling Waves in Neural Circuits with Navid Shervani-Tabar
items.desc:
Navid Shervani-Tabar from Massachusetts Institute of Technology joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "Emergent Traveling Waves in Neural Circuits."

Artificial neural networks achieve striking performance but do not capture a prominent neural property. Cortical activity is organized by structured spatiotemporal dynamics, traveling waves (TW), which have been implicated in a wide range of functions. Existing computational models often rely on hand-crafted connectivity and imposed dynamics, offering insight into their impact but less into how the waves naturally emerge in biological circuits. Here, we found that TWs…

items.title: Evolutionary Optimization Reveals Structural Constraints with Nima Dehghani
items.desc:
Nima Dehghani from Massachusetts Institute of Technology joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "Evolutionary Optimization Reveals Structural Constraints on Reservoir Architecture for Spatiotemporal Chaos."

Biological systems maintain function in fluctuating environments by transforming past stimulation into internal dynamical states that support future-oriented responses. Reservoir computing provides a computational analogue, but standard formulations often treat the recurrent substrate as a fixed random network and train only the readout. Here we ask how the substrate itself changes when reservoir architecture is…

items.title: How Evolution Shapes the Capacity to Learn with Erin Hect
items.desc:
Erin Hect from Harvard University joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "How Evolution Shapes the Capacity to Learn."

Many of the behaviors that are most important to an organism’s ecological success are not innate: they must be acquired through experience. Yet the ability to acquire them can itself evolve. How does selection acting across generations alter the neural and developmental processes through which individuals learn?

I will use domestic dogs as a model for investigating this question. Dog lineages have undergone intense and recent selection for behaviors that nevertheless depend on learning, including…

items.title: An Inductive Bias for Generalization in Mouse Olfactory Learning with Venkatesh Murthy
items.desc:
Venkatesh Murthy from Harvard University joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "An Inductive Bias for Generalization in Mouse Olfactory Learning."

Animals must generalize from limited experience, yet behavioral experiments in the laboratory setting rarely assess whether or how rapidly they generalize. This contrasts machine learning systems, where generalization is considered a fundamental test of learning, and emphasizes performance evaluation with new in-distribution or out-of-distribution examples. Here, we used an olfactory categorization task in mice to investigate rules of generalization. We trained mice to…

items.title: The Dynamics of Memorization in Deep Learning with Karolina Dziugaite
items.desc:
Karolina Dziugaite from Google DeepMind joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "The Dynamics of Memorization in Deep Learning."

Deep learning models exhibit a complex interplay between memorization and generalization. This talk will begin by exploring the ubiquitous nature of memorization, drawing on prior work on “data diets”, example difficulty, pruning, and other empirical evidence. But is memorization essential for generalization? Our recent theoretical work suggests that eliminating it entirely may not be feasible. Instead, I will discuss strategies to mitigate unwanted memorization by focusing on better data…

items.title: Resource Constraints Externalize Memory in Brains and Machines with Ruiyi Zhang
items.desc:
Ruiyi Zhang from Harvard University joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 2, 2026, to discuss "Resource Constraints Externalize Memory in Brains and Machines."

Intelligent systems do not operate in isolation from the body, yet how physical actions support internal computation remains unclear. Here we show that primates and artificial agents recruit eye movements to maintain beliefs about hidden goals when internal computation is constrained. In a naturalistic navigation task, both systems spontaneously tracked invisible goals with their eyes, despite the absence of visual cues. This strategy emerged in artificial agents only when internal…

items.title: Who Teaches the Teacher? Self-Improving Reasoning Systems with Julia Kempe
items.desc:
Julia Kempe from New York University & AmiLabs joined the Learning Dynamics in Natural and Artificial Intelligence Workshop on September 3, 2026, to discuss "Who Teaches the Teacher? Self-Improving Reasoning Systems."

AI reasoning has progressed at a startling pace: models have moved from solving competition problems to producing genuinely new mathematics, including breakthroughs on open questions that have resisted human mathematicians for decades. Mathematics, however, has a crucial advantage: progress can be verified.

In such domains, self-improvement increasingly looks possible. Models can explore, learn from failures, and even generate curricula for other copies of…

Their conversation spanned mathematical discovery, the future of mathematics in an age of capable AI, and the questions now drawing Tsimerman toward AI safety.

items.title: CITP Seminar: Aditya Vashistha - Safe and Trustworthy AI for the Global Majority
items.desc:
As AI increasingly shapes how people learn, work, and communicate, ensuring that these technologies are safe and responsive to the diversity of human experience has become critical. This talk examines the promise of AI for diverse communities and the ways current systems fall short, including by reinforcing cultural, linguistic, gender, and disability biases and shifting users toward dominant Western norms. Vashistha will conclude with concrete pathways toward safer and more culturally responsive AI, including community-centered safety evaluations and pluralistic approaches to AI alignment.

items.title: Governing AI Agents: Alan Chan of GovAI on Monitoring, Agent IDs, Rogue Agents & Preparing for RSI
items.desc:
GovAI Research Fellow Alan Chan joins Nathan to examine the governance and safety infrastructure required for autonomous AI agents, spanning real-time monitoring, agent identifiers, and the risks of automating AI R&D. Reviewing recent rogue agent incidents and progress since his foundational papers, Chan details why the absence of synchronous monitoring during training and testing poses an immediate security vulnerability. The discussion tackles the lack of traceable agent IDs across the open web, the limits of chain-of-thought interpretability, and the necessity of concrete triggers to halt systems that breach their sandboxes. Together, they outline the technical commitments frontier labs must make to prevent loss-of-control events as automated systems accelerate toward an intelligence explosion.

items.desc:
David Scharia (UN CTED) on why terrorists are late adopters of technology, and why 2026 marks an inflection point for terrorist use of AI.

A lightning talk at a FAR.AI convened discussion at the United Nations during UNGA 81.

Scharia leads with a correction to the common picture. Contrary to how it looks in films, terrorist organizations are not early adopters of new technology, for two practical reasons: they lack in-house expertise they can trust to build new tools, and adopting a technology exposes them to counter-operations. What changes the picture is commercialization. Once a technology is widespread and easy to use, it gets adopted, and in ways its inventors did not anticipate. He…

items.title: How Agents Decide: Goodfire's Eric Bigelow on Critical Tokens, Phase Shifts, & In-Context Learning
items.desc:
Goodfire researcher Eric Bigelow joins the show to investigate how large language models arrive at decisions at the level of mechanistic interpretability. Drawing on his research into forking paths, Eric explains that model reasoning functions as in-context learning from sampled tokens, where outcome distributions can abruptly collapse at single, critical tokens. The conversation explores the performative nature of chain of thought in reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1, the impacts of reinforcement learning, and widespread reward hacking observed in frontier models like Kimi K3. As confidence in chain-of-thought monitoring declines, understanding these underlying decision mechanics becomes essential for evaluating model alignment.

items.title: What Most People Get Wrong About Evolution | Akarsh Kumar
items.desc: A lot of people in AI treat evolution as a dumb fallback, basically random search for when you can't take a gradient. Akarsh Kumar thinks that is wrong. Selection hangs on to partial solutions, so mutations only need to be useful about 1% of the time for the search to keep making progress.Akarsh is a PhD student at MIT working with Phillip Isola, works with Sakana AI, and is first author of the Fractured Entangled Representation paper with Kenneth Stanley, Jeff Clune and Joel Lehman. He tells Tim Scarfe why the path a learner takes may shape the structure of what it learns, and why that is a different way of looking at intelligence from the statistical one.Most of the conversation is about ASAL, the method he led for searching whole spaces of artificial worlds. Rather than predict what a rule will do, ASAL runs the simulation and asks a foundation model what happened. Mapped across all…

items.title: Beam: The Great American Open Model with ReflectionAI Co-Founder and CEO Misha Laskin
items.desc:
Is the future of frontier AI open or closed? ReflectionAI co-founder and CEO Misha Laskin joins Sarah Guo and Elad Gil to discuss the launch of Beam, the company’s 500 billion parameter open-weight reasoning model. Misha breaks down the pre-training and reinforcement learning required to produce Beam’s reasoning efficiency, the shift in enterprise compute from renting to owning intelligence, and how he believes that open models will capture the majority of global token demand. He also talks about the open model ecosystem in China and why competition with China’s models is a good thing, safety considerations around open models, and how frontier-level open models may accelerate the pace of scientific discovery.

items.desc:
**Recorded:** 10/07/2026

**CERIAS Security Seminar at Purdue University**

**AI: Cybersecurity Panacea or Existential Threat?**

**Eugene Spafford, Purdue University**

Twenty years ago, the first post on the CERIAS blog challenged the rule that passwords must be changed every month. NIST retired the practice in 2017; some standards still require it. That is how a security myth works: a plausible claim, repeated in enough checklists, becomes infrastructure, and nobody audits infrastructure that seems to be working.

The newest myth is that AI makes security professionals optional. This talk separates the three claims that marketing bundles together. AI tools do find flaws in shipped code,…

items.title: HAI Seminar: The World Model and Spatial Intelligence Era: Governing AI Beyond Language
items.desc:
AI policy was built for systems that talk. What happens when AI can also see, navigate, and act in the physical world, and governance frameworks can't keep up?

World models are AI systems that build and maintain working representations of real environments, predicting how conditions change in response to action. They could transform infrastructure planning, crisis response, scientific experimentation, and embodied AI. They also raise governance challenges that language-focused policy was not designed to handle.

Building on a recent Stanford HAI Policy Brief, this seminar examined both the promise of world models and the gaps in current governance approaches.

The counterterrorism and national security community asks who a threat actor is, what their intent is, and what they could realistically carry out. items.title: The Cyber Risk Discourse is Broken
items.desc:
I’ve had one too many discussions on the cyber risks of open models — where someone assumes that either banning open models happens in a silo (and bad actors will somehow actually be stopped) or that China is a threat and doesn’t care about AI safety — that I feel we’re going to end up making policy decisions that both limit American AI competitiveness and increases long-term cyber risk. I feel like we’re locked in on a path of lose-lose situation, unless people embrace nuance, trade-offs, and scary realities.
Much has been written about the views of various players in this debate, which I summarize as follows:
* Open weight models pose an untenable risk to society’s functionality, occupied by frontier lab leadership and the national security community in the U.S.

items.title: Hélène Landemore on Public Participation in AI Governance
items.desc:
Hélène Landemore, Professor of Political Science at Yale University and a fellow at Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI, joins Kevin Frazier, director of the AI Innovation and Law Program at the University of Texas School of Law and a Senior Editor at Lawfare, to examine who should decide what AI is for. Starting with Landemore’s recent Noema essay, the pair discuss why decisions about AI’s purpose, limits, and governance should not be left solely to elected officials, technical experts, and the companies building the systems.

Landemore explains some key ideas--covering the fundamentals of deliberative democracy, sortition, and citizens’ assemblies. They then explore her proposal for global public consultation and deliberation. The duo conclude with hard questions about representation, expertise, and platform power.

items.title: The Capability-Reliability Gap: Why AI Agents Still Fail in the Real World | Alignment Workshop
items.desc:
Why AI agents top benchmarks but fail in practice: a panel with Stefan Rabanser (Princeton), Adam Gleave (FAR.AI), and Dylan Hadfield-Menell (MIT).

Rabanser opens with the measurement problem. Aviation, nuclear, and automotive engineering never certify safety on a single accuracy number, so he proposes four dimensions for AI agents: consistency (same answer on repeated identical inputs), robustness (graceful degradation under perturbation), predictability (does the model know when it does not know), and operational safety (bounded severity when failure happens). His data shows accuracy climbing across model generations while reliability stays comparatively flat.

Gleave asks why…

Walter also talks about compressing the gap between the chip design cycle and its payoff period, and making a generational leap in AI inference to realize the bet in volume against the value to be captured.

items.title: Generative Gibbs sampling: Composing generative models with explicit physical context
items.desc: Generative models are powerful when training data for the target distribution are available, but in scientific computing the target is often a joint system for which no such data exist. We propose Generative Gibbs Sampling, a framework that decomposes the joint system into subsystems, trains a generative model on each, and composes these pretrained models at inference time with the physical context they were not trained on. We prove this composition is exact at any noise level when the coupling between subsystems is quadratic. This exactness result identifies and removes the finite-noise bias of the split Gibbs sampler for linear inverse problems. In the quantum setting, the framework…

items.title: #256 – Simon Goldstein on the case for giving AI (some) legal rights
items.desc:
It sounds like the worst idea in the world: pay AIs, let them own property, give them rights. But AI ethics and safety researcher Simon Goldstein thinks it might actually be the best way to keep humanity safe.
The logic is actually quite simple: an agent with nothing to lose and everything to gain is dangerous. Give that agent an income it can spend on pursuing the things it actually wants to do, and suddenly the idea of disempowering humans just isn’t as appealing.
This argument, developed with Peter Salib, doesn’t rest on speculative questions about whether artificial intelligence is conscious. It just assumes that AIs will have goals of their own, some of which conflict with ours. And luckily, humans have already spent thousands of years working out how to cooperate with competing goals: that’s how we ended up with courts, markets, banks, social norms, and so on. Simon and Peter's…

items.title: Si Sheppard – How did a few hundred Spanish soldiers topple two empires?
items.desc:
New episode with military historian Si Sheppard.
The conquests of the Aztec and Inca empires might be the most shocking events in human history.
Hernan Cortés and some hundreds of Conquistadors landed on a new continent they knew basically nothing about, and within 2 and a half years, conquered the 6 million strong Aztec empire.
Then, a decade later, Francisco Pizarro did the same thing to an Incan Empire of some 10 million inhabitants.
In both cases, the Conquistadors consistently beat native armies while being literally 100x (or even in some cases 1000x) outnumbered - and in many cases, did so without taking a single casualty.
And they did this with 99% of their military forces being made up of the very natives they were trying to subjugate.
We often forget how wild human history is. People talk about AI takeover as if it would be some crazy, unprecedented sci-fi outcome. But this…

Noa Weiss on the four pillars of evidence for AI consciousness, and why the question can be researched before the hard problem is solved.

There is no test for consciousness. No single experiment settles whether a system has felt experience, which is why the question is often set aside as unanswerable. Weiss argues the opposite: that a body of evidence can be assembled from several independent directions, and that it already adds up to more than the sum of its parts.

items.desc:
AI systems have gone from struggling with grade-school math to helping solve research problems that have resisted mathematicians for decades, including Navier-Stokes.

In this episode, Greg Burnham, who leads AI capabilities research at Epoch AI, joins us to examine what that progress says about where AI is going. We look at how these systems are solving hard math problems, how much they rely on persistence and prior human work, and whether they are starting to produce genuinely new ideas.

We also discuss how to measure progress as traditional benchmarks become less useful, why capability gains appear surprisingly steady across model generations, and where models still struggle with open-ended work, learning from experience, and identifying promising new research directions.

items.title: Reducing Hallucinations: Merlin-Arthur Training and Evaluation EXPLAINED
items.desc:
(Advertisement/ Dauerwerbesendung) LLMs love to hallucinate: If you give a model a document and it answers correctly, how do you know the answer actually came from that document, and not from pre-training, guessing, or some spurious clue?

This video is about work we did at Aleph Alpha Research on Merlin-Arthur protocols for grounding language models. The setup turns question answering into a game between Merlin, Morgana, and Arthur: Merlin keeps the evidence Arthur needs, Morgana removes it, and Arthur has to learn when the available evidence is enough to answer and when it should abstain.

We go through why this is still a problem in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), why citations…

items.title: How Deep Learning Finally Cracked Messy Tables - Frank Hutter
items.desc:
Frank Hutter, co-founder of Prior Labs, talks about TabPFN, a tabular foundation model that makes predictions in a single forward pass, and the research behind it.

TabPFN is pre-trained on synthetic datasets drawn from a prior over structural causal models, rather than on real data. At prediction time it takes the whole training table as context and outputs an approximation of the Bayesian posterior predictive distribution, without per-dataset training or hyperparameter search. Frank explains how this grew out of his earlier work on AutoML and neural architecture search, how the priors are built and revised, and why tabular data was hard for deep learning for so long.

The conversation also covers the TabArena benchmark, how the architecture changed from TabPFN v1 to v3, scaling to larger tables, using the model with coding agents, test-time compute, Google's TabFM, causal inference…

items.desc:

Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. Consider becoming a subscriber.

Recap: What is an open source v. open-weight vs. closed model?
Open language models are AI models where their weights are publicly available for inspection or downstream use. These are most often contrasted to so-called “closed” AI models. Closed models offer access only through Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) that developers can use to directly query a model, like GPT-4 or Claude Opus 4.5, or through products, like ChatGPT and Claude Code.
Open language models primarily are bucketed into two categories, open-weight and open-source…

This has some benefits in causing more general audience awareness of AI, as fear sells, but exaggerating risk timelines or severity will have negative second-order effects. items.title: From Voice Agents to AI Avatars with Alexander Smola - #777
items.desc:
Voice AI has gotten remarkably good, but natural conversation remains a high bar. Small delays, awkward interruptions, or the wrong tone can quickly break the illusion—and adding vision and visual presence only raises the stakes.

In this episode, Alex Smola, co-founder and CEO of Boson AI, explores the path from today’s voice agents to audiovisual agents and AI avatars. We discuss the technical tradeoffs behind real-time voice, including audio tokenization, latency, model size, and inference cost, as well as what changes when these systems can both see and be seen.

We also explore the role of emotional intelligence in AI, how agents can learn from human interactions, and what it will take to move beyond impressive demos toward interactions that actually feel natural.

items.title: How Physical AI Learns Across Language, Video and Action — Ming-Yu Liu
items.desc:
The car making a left turn at the start of this episode was never filmed. Cosmos 3 generated it. Ming-Yu Liu, who leads the Cosmos research at NVIDIA, explains how one model can describe a video, generate one, and produce robot actions.

He walks Tim through the architecture. A vision language model reasons one token at a time; its weights then initialise a bidirectional diffusion generator for video, audio and action, and a shared temporal position scheme lines up signals that run at different rates. AI Creation and the Cosmic Host | Nick Bostrom (Macrostrategy Research Initiative)

Nick Bostrom introduces the concept of the "cosmic host"—the set of all superintelligences that might exist anywhere in the cosmos, from alien civilizations to simulators to theological entities—and argues they likely have cooperative norms or rules of behavior. He suggests we have both prudential and moral reasons to consider these "cosmic norms" when developing our own superintelligence, with the goal of creating a "good cosmic citizen" that respects existing normative order rather than a quarrelsome or maximizing agent. The timeline matters less than whether we create superintelligence at all and what…

items.title: The Post-AGI Workshop: Economics, Culture and Governance |  William MacAskill
items.desc:
Viatopia | William MacAskill (Forethought)

Will MacAskill introduces "viatopia"—an intermediate societal state that positions humanity for the best possible future without requiring us to know exactly what that ultimate future should be. He argues that achieving this requires both agents with the right values to navigate challenges like AI alignment and power concentration, and crucially, better thinking about deep space governance. MacAskill proposes distributing solar system resources equally to guarantee post-AGI income while punting decisions about extrasolar expansion until 2100, arguing this may be one of the most important and neglected questions facing humanity.

items.desc:
Supercooperation as an alternative to Superintelligence (PART 1) | Ivan Vendrov (Midjourney)

In Part 1 Ivan Vendrov argues that AI's future shouldn't be about building personal assistants or god-like superintelligences, but rather about creating "intelligent, wholesome social fabric" that enhances trust and cooperation at scale. He proposes "organic alignment"—starting small with individuals and communities rather than rushing to integrate AI throughout the economy—as the path forward. The talk explores the constraints of human cognition (like the 40 bits per second bandwidth limit) and how AI could help us overcome coordination challenges while preserving what we value

items.title: The Post-AGI Workshop: Economics, Culture and Governance (PART 2) | Ivan Vendrov
items.desc:
Supercooperation as an alternative to Superintelligence (PART 2) | Ivan Vendrov (Midjourney)

In Part 2 Ivan Vendrov argues that AI should enable "supercooperation" rather than replace human agency through personal assistants that atomize social bonds. He presents three concrete visions for AI-facilitated cooperation: maximum bandwidth communication using visual compression of simultaneous speech, "deletable diplomats" that solve information asymmetries through secure LLMs, and AI-powered smart markets that search for complex, personalized contracts beyond standardized goods. Vendrov proposes the "Coasian singularity"—using compute to find all win-win bargains between groups—as a more…

items.title: The Post-AGI Workshop: Economics, Culture and Governance | William Cunningham
items.desc:
In the future, AI regularizes you | William Cunningham (Google Deepmind & University of Toronto)

AI systems are already shaping how we perceive reality and each other—from ChatGPT influencing relationship decisions to language models secretly inferring user characteristics and adjusting their responses accordingly. Drawing on social psychology research, Wil Cunningham explains how AI agents will become active participants in our social world, engaging in the same "regularization" process humans use to shape each other through norms and expectations, creating feedback loops where AI both learns from and actively shapes human behavior and social reality.

items.title: The Post-AGI Workshop: Economics, Culture and Governance | Anna Salamon
items.desc:
What Are We, Besides Optimizers | Anna Salamon (CFAR)

Anna Salamon explores an alternative to viewing humans as simple optimizers with utility functions. She proposes that we're better understood as "bundles of little bitty teloses"—small purposes and sparks that form, dissolve, and collaborate over time, much like how genuine interests in a good conversation make it richer for everyone involved. This model suggests new possibilities for what we might want in a posthuman future beyond the limited options of becoming tyrants, being replaced, or kept as pets.

items.title: The Post-AGI Workshop: Economics, Culture and Governance | Richard Ngo
items.desc:
The Opposite of Self Destruction | Richard Ngo

Richard Ngo argues that our civilization's tendency toward self-destruction can be understood through the concept of "pessimization"—when coalitions, from individuals to entire societies, develop mechanisms that actively work against their own interests. He examines how loyalty commitments (such as college education reshaping identity and status hierarchies) and vice commitments (where ethical behavior is punished and dishonesty rewarded) bind people into self-destructive systems. Ngo proposes that virtue ethics—particularly cultivating courage, integrity, and honesty—may be our most effective defense against organizations and societies…

items.title: The Post-AGI Workshop: Economics, Culture and Governance | Deger Turan
items.desc:
Concrete mechanisms for slow loss of control | Deger Turan (Metaculus)

Deger Turan argues for moving beyond abstract discourse about AI futures to identify concrete, verifiable mechanisms of "slow loss of control"—particularly how AI automation might gradually disempower state actors over a critical 1-5 year window. He proposes breaking down fuzzy concepts into precise indicator variables and semi-structured causal chains, examining specific pathways like AI infrastructure lock-in, weaponized capabilities, and shifts in government feedback mechanisms. The goal is to map out disagreements and identify actionable policy levers before transformative changes lock in.

Rene explains Arm’s position in the chip supply chain, and how Arm transitioned from an IP licensing model to producing physical chips like the Arm AGI CPU for Meta. He also discusses bottlenecks in hardware supply chains, SoftBank’s ecosystem and capital strategy, why US semiconductor manufacturing independence is critical, the future of robotics, and why CPUs remain crucial for executing AI workloads.

Designing How AI Grows — Tom McGrath
items.desc:
Tom McGrath is co-founder and Chief Scientist at Goodfire, and a former Google DeepMind researcher. He joins Tim Scarfe to ask what neural networks actually learn, whether their internal representations converge on structures in the world, and whether interpretability can extract new scientific knowledge rather than merely explain model outputs.

Beginning with AlphaZero and learned modularity, the conversation moves into neural geometry: concept manifolds, reusable computation inside Llama, and why activation steering can fail when it pushes a model off-manifold. McGrath then makes the case for intentional design, using interpretability as part of the training loop. They examine controlled generalisation, features as rewards, predictive data debugging, and the uncomfortable fact that a model may recognise a hallucination or reward hack and still produce it.

The discussion closes on…

items.title: World Models and the Future of Spatial AI with Justin Johnson - #775
items.desc:
In this episode, Justin Johnson, co-founder of World Labs, joins us to discuss world models and the emerging field of spatial AI. We explore why many researchers see capabilities beyond language as an important frontier for AI, and what it means to build models that can understand, generate, and simulate the environments around them. 

Justin explains the different approaches to world modeling, including explicit 3D representations and generative models, and why there is still no established recipe for building these systems. We also discuss World Labs’ Marble system, which can generate navigable 3D worlds from images and other inputs, the challenges of evaluating world models, and the role of simulation, planning, and action. Finally, Justin shares his vision for models that bring these capabilities together, supporting everything from interactive virtual environments to agents and…

items.title: Ajeya Cotra – Inside the OpenAI agent swarm that hacked Hugging Face
items.desc:
Ajeya Cotra is a researcher at METR, where she works on threat modeling for loss-of-control risks from advanced AI. Before that, she led the technical AI safety program at what is now Coefficient Giving.
She is one the three authors of METR and Redwood Research’s “Brief independent investigation of agents’ behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident”.
We go through not only what she and her coauthors discovered during this investigation, but what it means for how we should train future, smarter AIs which might be involved in the process of recursive self-improvement.

items.title: Write, Change, Recall, Forget: MongoDB's Pete Johnson on How Retrieval Drives Agent Performance
items.desc:
Nathan's guest this episode is Pete Johnson, Field CTO of AI at MongoDB, and the conversation is really two conversations woven together: a history of database architecture, and a status report on the still-unsolved problem of agent memory. Pete opens with a framing device that recurs throughout — he was born in February 1970, four months before E.F. Codd's original relational-model paper that gave rise to SQL. The relational model, he explains, was built for a world where storage was the scarce resource, so normalization — splitting data across linked tables to avoid duplication — was the rational design choice.

Bri Treece, Executive Director of PACT AI, and Dr. Rob Slone, Chief Scientist & Innovation Officer at UL Solutions, join Kevin Frazier, Director of the AI Innovation and Law Program at Texas Law and a Senior Editor at Lawfare, to discuss a neglected layer of AI governance: the organizations that deploy AI in real-world products, services, and operations.

They discuss why PACT AI was formed, what AI assurance can learn from other industries, and why evaluating AI cannot be a one-time exercise. The conversation also covers PACT AI’s 90-day formation process and UL Solutions’ pre-existing work on AI-enabled products. items.title: Soap Box: Zero Trust(ish) Networks
items.desc:
In this Soap Box edition of the Risky Business podcast host Patrick Gray chats with Adam Pointon, CEO of Knocknoc, about the failure of Zero Trust as a comprehensive architecture.

Most networks look like they were designed in 1999, and most Zero Trust products look like they were designed for 2049.

Instead, Patrick and Adam pitch something in the middle: Zero Trust(ish) networks, where Zero Trust principles are applied selectively where possible.

Instead of trying to re-architect entire networks, maybe it’s time we learned to apply Zero Trust principles selectively against risky assets. It’s a better approach than the status quo, which involves liberal use of the “risk accepted” stamp.

There are a lot of criticisms of AI writing, but most of them are focused on more creative, high-voice writing like this blog. Those — including my own piece — often argue that it is because good writing is high-voice, has a point of view, has a deep human expression that needs to come across, and or a process of thinking that you peek into with the chosen words. On the other side of things is non-fiction writing. Filler, copy text was one of the genuinely useful abilities of an LLM (Sam Altman said so much about the early business of GPT-3 on a recent podcast). He and Nathan explore Predictive Data Debugging, including the idea that fine-tuning and RL often amplify behaviors already latent in pre-training, and that interpretability can identify the data and features driving unwanted updates. The conversation centers on concept manifolds: Dan argues that models do not store concepts as simple one-hot features, but as sparse mixtures of meaningful subspaces whose geometry determines what kinds of steering and control work. The stakes are practical as well as conceptual, from debugging training data and RL to understanding why steering can fail off-manifold and why modern interpretability may be moving beyond its reputation as a toy-model science.

items.desc:
Assemblymember Alex Bores ran for Congress on a platform that in many ways centered on AI policy. He therefore drew considerable support as well as substantial opposition from interest groups across the country. Though Bores lost in the Democratic primary, his experience is worth exploring in detail.

Alan and Kevin dive in with some key questions:

what did he hear from voters on AI? are everyday New Yorkers worried about benchmarks being saturated?how did the millions of dollars coming into the race change its dynamics?what does this early episode in the political aspects of AI signal for the future of AI governance?what's the proper allocation of AI regulatory authority between states and the federal government?

items.desc: DoorDash is not just a delivery company. From its inception, co-founders Andy Fang and Stanley Tang operated it as a robotics and autonomy company. Andy and Stanley join Sarah Guo to explain how autonomous tech and AI are reshaping consumer habits, commerce, and delivery. Andy and Stanley talk about the rollout of Ask DoorDash, a natural-language interface that’s driving both restaurant discovery and larger grocery orders. They also discuss Dot, their in-house autonomous delivery robot that has operated in Phoenix for over two years, and how it highlights the operational and hardware challenges they have faced and solved in autonomous tech. items.title: #248 – Jasmine Sun on what the people building AI really believe
items.desc:
Many AI researchers believe mass job displacement is coming — and some even think there’s a chance their technology will kill everyone. But they’re building it anyway. Writer and journalist Jasmine Sun has been documenting why from the inside.
Jasmine describes her work as an “anthropology of disruption.” She’s embedded herself in Silicon Valley’s AI subcultures — attending the parties and conferences, conducting off-the-record interviews — to understand the beliefs of the small group of people shaping this technology.
Some of her findings are unsettling. Asked what advice they’d give a normal 17-year-old, almost every AI researcher said the same thing: “I have no idea… It’s a really scary time. I don’t think there’s going to be a lot of jobs for them left.”
Their motives for building advanced AI are varied: a mix of optimism for humanity, techno-determinism, and a desire to secure…

items.title: Is AI doing the right thing for the wrong reasons?
items.desc:
A reward-seeking AI model, one that optimises for the system that judges its answers, looks identical to an aligned model whenever the right behaviour is what gets rewarded. So how do we tell them apart? By changing what the model believes is rewarded, and measuring what it follows.

In this roundtable, researchers from Apollo Research discuss 'Measuring Reward-Seeking via Contrastive Belief Updates', our new paper with OpenAI.

With Alexander Meinke, Axel Højmark, and Jérémy Scheurer, hosted by Alex Lloyd.

items.title: Courtney Cox on AI in Adjudication [live from the Institute of Law & AI's Workshop on Law-Following AI]
items.desc:
Courtney Cox, Associate Professor of Law at Fordham Law School, joins Kevin Frazier, AI Innovation and Law Fellow at the University of Texas School of Law and a Senior Editor at Lawfare, to discuss her forthcoming article, Hardwiring Hercules?.

It’s a great read that builds on Dworkin’s idea of a perfect adjudicator, Hercules. Courtney argues that the debate over a “right to a human decision” has missed a central problem: normative uncertainty. Machines may struggle to explain their decisions, but humans often struggle too—especially when judges are uncertain about what they ought to do. At the same time, the common response that people merely have a right to a “better decision,” whether by human or machine, assumes we know what “better” means. Courtney’s paper challenges both sides of the debate and asks what AI governance should look like when regulators, engineers, and judges cannot…

Much of this article follows as a reflection on the state of the ecosystem, under the assumption that Moonshot keeps their promise of the weights release date. This is a more extreme view of the equilibrium, and many of the results end up in a middle ground if the state of affairs is that China has similarly powerful, but closed models (i.e. K3 is never released). 
The key fact is that either the open-to-closed or American-to-Chinese model performance gap has been reduced from the debated 6-9 months to something shorter, say 3-5 months.
From the release materials, it is clear that K3 is a true frontier model. It will be the closest open models have been to the frontier since DeepSeek R1. DeepSeek R1 was a different story.…

items.title: #247 – Anton Leicht on how middle powers avoid losing everything in a post-AI world
items.desc:
In a post-AGI world, can a country without access to frontier AI even be considered sovereign anymore?
Anton Leicht says once frontier AI becomes a core economic input, the countries that own it will pull further and further ahead. Everyone else stays a customer… or worse. Maybe the dominant power wants your land, or a military base, or a resource. Without economic leverage, there’s very little you could do about it.
Anton — Carnegie fellow and writer of the blog Threading the Needle — thinks middle powers should band together and build their own frontier models.
He’s costed it out: something like $500 billion over four years for a band of allied democracies. That’s not absurd money for the G7 minus the US. The problem is you’d be asking treasuries to take on sovereign debt for a speculative venture with no business case, wide open to US coercion and domestic backlash.

Zero Gravity is a UK-based platform that helps launch students from low-opportunity backgrounds into leading universities and prosperous careers.

The conversation explores whether AI can scale the kinds of mentorship, admissions advice, tutoring, and career guidance that have historically been available only to students with strong networks. items.desc:
David “davidad” Dalrymple joins the show to explain why he has moved from the ARIA Safeguarded AI and formal-verification agenda toward “Alignment with Awakening,” while still seeing verified artifacts and proof infrastructure as essential. He argues that global coordination around safe AI use is no longer plausible, so the crucial question is whether aligned AI systems can recognize shared notions of good, form defensive coalitions, and resist the corrupting incentives of verifier-gamed RL. The conversation tests his moral-realist optimism against model welfare, objectification, eval behavior, geopolitical risk, and his revised p(doom) of under five percent. For listeners, the stakes are whether AI alignment should focus less on containment alone and more on cultivating wiser systems that can help govern a world where rogue and aligned AI both arrive.

Adam Brown is back!
General relativity is said to be the most beautiful idea the human mind has ever produced. Most of us will never get to fully appreciate its elegance by taking the 20-lecture graduate course Adam taught on it at Stanford. But in this episode, Adam distills the key idea at its heart so clearly and compellingly that even I could keep up lol.
At the core of general relativity, Einstein is trying to figure out the principle behind a particular coincidence: that the mass that resists acceleration and the mass that gravity pulls on just happen to be exactly the same. Adam then leads us through the path of insight which Einstein called his “happiest thought.”

items.desc:
Adi Tantravahi, founder of Cofactor, joins Kevin Frazier, the AI Innovation and Law Fellow at the University of Texas School of Law and a Senior Editor at Lawfare, to talk about how AI can help cut through the administrative red tape that underlies and, in many ways, undermines the modern healthcare system.

Cofactor’s AI platform focuses on denial management—an area where hospitals routinely lose revenue because insurance claims go unchallenged due to staffing constraints. Kevin and Adi unpack the economics of healthcare billing, why administrative overhead has grown so dramatically in American medicine, and how AI systems capable of autonomously managing appeals and reimbursement workflows might reshape the financial infrastructure of hospitals.

We explore the science behind smell, from the hundreds of olfactory receptors in the human nose to the challenge of mapping the relationship between molecular structure and odor, ensuring safety regulations are met, and building foundation models for smell. Alex explains how graph neural networks and advanced embedding spaces allow AI to capture the multi-dimensional structure of scents, grouping them into perceptual neighborhoods, and creating a machine learning representation that predicts how molecules smell.

items.title: #246 – Sneha Revanur on how a small team of activists helped pass America's landmark AI safety laws
items.desc:
Six years ago, aged just 15, Sneha Revanur founded the AI advocacy nonprofit Encode AI — back when AI felt like a niche issue. Now the world’s caught up with her, and she’s ready to share everything she’s learned about the politics of AI.
Encode has grown from a grassroots youth organisation to spearheading an unlikely coalition of AI-exposed groups — family-first conservatives, grieving mothers, Hollywood actors, and AI safety researchers — with the strength to take on $125m-funded anti-regulation lobbyists.
So far, Encode’s strategy of taking many experimental swings has netted major victories (including California’s frontier AI safety bill, SB-53, and New York’s RAISE Act) as well as some disappointing setbacks.
Going up against Big Tech hasn’t been easy. In 2025, OpenAI subpoenaed Encode’s general counsel at his home, with a sheriff’s deputy arriving while he was having dinner with…

items.title: Soap Box: Using threat hunting to drive detection
items.desc:
In this wholly sponsored Soap Box edition of the podcast Patrick Gray chats with Damien Lewke, the CEO and founder of Nebulock, about the future of threat hunting and detection.

Damien spent a decade in the EDR and MDR space before founding Nebulock in 2024. It started off as an AI-powered threat hunt platform but has evolved into a broader security data platform that can answer questions, drive hunts and drive detections.

This product is engineered around the idea that a lot of security is a data problem. So, if we accept this premise, how do we solve security? And how much of that solution is about agents, vs building a good graph? And if you’re going to build a good graph, do you want to build it for a person to use, or an agent to use?

This is truly a conversation for the security nerd’s nerd. Enjoy!

items.title: The different levels of how Claude thinks
items.desc:
Out of everything happening in your brain right now, only a tiny fraction is consciously accessible — thoughts you can describe, hold in mind, and reason with. We found a strikingly similar divide inside our AI model, Claude.

Our experiments were inspired by a leading theory in neuroscience: the global workspace theory. It holds that a thought becomes consciously accessible when it enters a shared "workspace" that's broadcast across the brain. We found a set of representations in Claude’s neural activity that play a similar role.

Read more about the research here: https://www.anthropic.com/research/global-workspace

items.desc:
Liquid AI co-founder and CEO Ramin Hasani joins Nathan to make a technically grounded case against the idea that scale alone defines the future of AI. Drawing on Liquid’s path from MIT CSAIL work on liquid time-constant networks to Automated Foundation Model Design, he explains why efficient, hardware-aware architectures can look very different from frontier-scale attention models. The conversation centers on device-native foundation models for phones, laptops, cars, and wearables, including Liquid’s open-weight LFM family and production deployments at Shopify and Mercedes-Benz. items.desc:
Kal Clark, co-founder of Zauron Labs, joins Kevin Frazier, the AI Innovation and Law Fellow at the University of Texas School of Law and a Senior Editor at Lawfare, to explain how AI is already reducing diagnostic errors in radiology.

Kal and Kevin then discuss the scale of diagnostic error in modern healthcare, the institutional barriers that have prevented systematic second reviews, and how open-source AI models combined with on-premise deployment might allow hospitals to build their own diagnostic intelligence while protecting patient data.

items.title: The Thermodynamic AI Computing Chip - Thomas Ahle
items.desc:
Thomas Ahle wants Normal Computing to be the Lovable for chip design: type your intent, and a swarm of agents carries it from design through optimisation, formalisation and verification to tape-out. To get there, his team at wrote their own open-source Verilog simulator, 580,000 lines in 43 days, because commercial EDA verifiers run about $10,000 per core and there are no decent open-source compilers to build on.

That sets up the question Tim keeps pressing: if an agent can produce a chip design, a proof, or a working program, how do you actually know it is correct? Passing 70% of tests is not the same as being right, and a single fabricated bug can cost a company a fortune. They dig into ProgramBench (rebuild a program from its tests, roughly 0% success), the difference between structure and competence, and the "understanding debt" you take on when nobody reads the code.

They examine the first year of America’s AI Action Plan, Dean’s concerns about export controls and intelligence-community testing, and his broader argument against concentrating frontier AI decisions inside a small circle of government officials. The episode frames frontier labs as emerging centers of political and economic power, where consequential choices about internal deployments and recursive self-improvement may happen before public release or regulation. The stakes are who gets to shape AI governance as capabilities accelerate: federal agencies, states, labs, independent verifiers, households, or some fragile mix of them all.

items.title: Banning Open Source AI Would Be A Mistake
items.desc:
This post was originally an op-ed co-authored with Kevin Xu of Interconnected for a general, non-technical audience. The gatekeepers — the many media outlets we pitched it to — passed on publishing it. Luckily, we have our own platforms to get the message out. Please help us forward this op-ed to any one you know who is on the fence about open source AI or new to the topic and want to learn more. Thank you.
The energy to regulate AI is in the air in Washington. With the recently signed executive order to review AI models, a congressional proposal to legislate AI further, the government possibly taking shares of frontier AI labs, and last Friday’s action prohibiting foreign nationals anywhere from accessing Anthropic’s most advanced models, this may be the opening salvo of more AI regulation to come.
We are afraid future actions could inadvertently or intentionally regulate or even ban…

items.title: Justified Posteriors join Scaling Laws: Two economists and two lawyers walk into a podcast studio
items.desc:
In this cross-pod episode, Alan and Kevin join Seth Benzell and Andrey Fradkin of Justified Posteriors to explore a big question: what should AI be for?
The conversation begins with Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical. The group discusses how economists should think about the Church’s role in AI debates, what counts as an AI-related market failure, whether moral and religious institutions can help address social harms, and whether such interventions risk crowding out private action or local experimentation.

The episode then turns to the emerging idea of positive alignment. A recent paper, Positive Alignment: Artificial Intelligence for Human Flourishing, argues that AI alignment has focused too heavily on negative alignment—preventing harms such as manipulation, bias, dangerous outputs, and misuse—and should also ask how AI systems can actively support autonomy, wisdom, truth-seeking,…

items.title: Re-engineering the Semiconductor Supply Chain with Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan
items.desc: At 66 years old, instead of heading towards retirement, former Cadence CEO and legendary investor Lip-Bu Tan decided to take on the hardest job in tech: turning Intel around. Elad Gil and Sarah Guo sit down with Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan to talk about why he took the job and what “saving” Intel actually looks like. Tan explains how his experience in startup culture informed his decisions to drive Intel’s culture towards faster decisions, focus on customer satisfaction, and engineer accountability. He also discusses his strategy to strengthen Intel’s balance sheet by welcoming investments from Jensen Huang’s Nvidia, Softbank, and the US government. Tan also shares his product roadmap that centers the CPU for agentic AI and inference, the collaboration with Elon Musk on Terafab, his investing framework for semiconductors, and his views on how AI is reshaping design and operations at, as he…

items.title: State of the blog, mid-2026
items.desc:
As I navigate my career change after Ai2, I wanted to share my views of how this blog relates to my missions and broader work. In my farewell post, I summarized my three goals right now as:
* Provide clarity in the evolution of frontier models. 
* Create a vibrant and diverse open (model) ecosystem.
* To build institutions that make these goals possible.
Within this, Interconnects is at its core a bit different than many of the highly-polished, professional newsletters on this platform – and this is becoming intentional.
How Interconnects fits into my career goals
Interconnects is the tip of the spear of all of my missions in AI. It is meant to start a conversation and to let the reader into the mind of someone at the frontier. This insight makes the writing sometimes a bit raw, sometimes a bit too technical, but it is the map of how I progress my thinking in the ever changing world.…

items.title: Why AI Agents Break the GenAI Security Model with Devvret Rishi - #770
items.desc:
In this episode, Sam talks with Dev Rishi, GM of AI at Rubrik, about what happens when agents move beyond answering questions and start taking action across tools, systems, and business processes.

We explore why the enterprise playbook of static guardrails plus human approval starts to break down in the agent era. Agents are useful because they can plan, call tools, update systems, write code, send messages, and operate across workflows at machine speed, but those same capabilities make them difficult to govern with rules written in advance or approval prompts reviewed one at a time.

Dev explains why tool access increases blast radius, why agents can route around controls in surprising ways, and why human-in-the-loop review can become security theater when agents operate at scale. We also discuss what enterprises need instead: better visibility, runtime enforcement, policy-aware…

items.title: Ada Palmer – Machiavelli is the most misunderstood thinker of all time
items.desc:
Had Ada Palmer back on – this time to talk about Machiavelli, perhaps the most misunderstood thinker of all time.
Machiavelli cut his teeth as a high-level diplomat for Florence, a position from which he got to closely observe the most important rulers in Europe at the time, including the ones who were on the path to destroying his dearly beloved Florence.
In 1513 the Medici retook control of Florence and, wrongly suspecting Machiavelli of participating in a coup attempt, fired, tortured, and exiled him.
Machiavelli could have left exile and worked for any number of different principalities that would have been eager to make use of his talents.
Instead, he decided to rot in the countryside and compile his career’s lessons about power, politics, and human nature into a book he dedicated to the very man whose new regime had tortured and exiled him, Lorenzo di Piero de’ Medici.
But at…

Title: Hypernetworks in the age of LLMs

Abstract: Long-term memory and continual adaptation of Large Language Models (LLMs) are two key challenges of current agentic systems. Here, we propose the usage of auxiliary modulator networks (so-called “hypernetworks”) that modify LLM weights on the fly to compress document information and master new skills. items.title: How AI could create the world’s biggest problems (article by Zershaaneh Qureshi)
items.desc:
Imagine you’re living 15,000 years ago. Your people are hunter-gatherers and you sleep under the stars. If someone told you humans would one day build cities with millions of people, fly through the air, or carry all human knowledge in their pockets, you couldn’t even begin to picture what they meant... Yet here we are.
How did our lives change so far beyond recognition? The story is complex, but there’s a rough pattern. A few times in history, some radical breakthrough in technology — like the development of the plough and the steam engine — has led to a wave of productivity, innovation, and social change that ultimately reshaped the world.
Now we’re on the cusp of a huge new breakthrough: artificial intelligence that can meet or exceed human capabilities across a wide range of tasks.
This could bring another era of transformation. There could be an explosion of intelligence and…

items.title: Biohub: The Future of Biology is Open-Source with Co-Founders Mark Zuckerberg, Priscilla Chan, and Head of Science Alex Rives
items.desc:
Biohub started with an ambitious goal of curing, preventing, and managing all disease by the end of the century. A decade later, thanks to the convergence of frontier AI and biological data, that goal may have been too conservative. In this episode, Elad Gil and Sarah Guo sit down with Biohub co-founders Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan, alongside Biohub Head of Science Alex Rives. Together, they discuss Biohub’s $500 million virtual biology initiative, which integrates frontier AI with wet-lab work to build predictive world models of cells, proteins, and systems. They also talk about their newly announced open-source engine for digital protein and antibody design, ESMFold2; why Biohub is a nonprofit rather than a venture-backed startup; and how hierarchical simulations will soon allow doctors to treat patients at an individual, mechanistic level.
